attribution.note: Zitron's own sentence in his newsletter. He states it as his own analysis, not as a quote.

semantics.note: The normalised text keeps 'every single AI startup', 'will need' and the 'which means' link. Treating it as causal is reasonable because the funding need is presented as following from the payment problem.

contract.note: Reading 'cannot afford' as unable to pay from operating receipts fits the context. Limiting the claim to model-buying startups while keeping the universal scope is fair. The support and contradiction tests follow his words.

evidence.note: April 2026 report on Cursor's fundraising and slight positive gross margin. It gives no operating cash flow and does not show that outside funding is needed to pay model bills.
Stripe says Gamma reached $100M ARR profitably. This is an unverified company disclosure with no model-bill data and no profit definition, so it does not meet the contradiction test.

reviews.rationale: The packet does not identify the labs' largest customers, their cash flows or model-bill histories, and nothing shows the labs need quarterly increases. The Gamma item hints at an exception but is not verified and does not show rising model payments funded internally. The evidence neither establishes nor disproves the claimed necessity.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his newsletter, introduced as 'a reminder'.

semantics.note: Faithful. 'Both' and the 'tens of billions a year' threshold are kept. 'Woefully' is emphasis.

contract.note: The speaker names no loss measure, and the result depends on which one is used. For 2025, GAAP net loss is above $20B for both labs. Anthropic's operating loss ($8.1B) and OpenAI's loss excluding non-cash items ($8B) are below it. The contract leaves the basis unknown and withholds a verdict, which is a cautious choice.

evidence.note: Audited OpenAI 2025 figures, verified by the FT: operating loss $20.9B and net loss $38.5B, both above the threshold. Most of the net loss comes from a conversion-related fair-value charge.
Anthropic's S-1 shows a 2025 net loss of $42.0B but an operating loss of only $8.1B. The gap is a $34.3B fair-value charge, so the result depends on the measure.
Per the FT's source, OpenAI's 2025 loss excluding non-cash items was $8B, below the threshold. This is a different measure from net loss.

reviews.rationale: On GAAP net loss, both labs lost more than $20B in 2025. On operating or cash-like measures, Anthropic (and OpenAI on the adjusted figure) lost well under $20B; the net figures are driven by non-cash fair-value charges. The speaker gave no basis and the contract withholds a verdict for that reason, so the outcome depends on an interpretation he did not supply.

attribution.note: Zitron's own assertion in his newsletter.

semantics.note: Faithful. 'Neither', 'only' and the low cost of signing contracts are all kept. The explicit 'only... because' makes the causal kind right.

contract.note: Reading 'obligations' as payments as they fall due matches 'keep up'. The contract flags the lifetime-commitment reading as an ambiguity. Requiring matched liquidity and payment schedules is fair.

evidence.note: Anthropic announced $65B of Series H funding in May 2026. This is a company disclosure and shows neither remaining cash nor whether payments as they fall due are covered.
Reported figure of $73B+ OpenAI cash at March 2026, from the quarter before the target period. There is no payment schedule to compare it against.
The S-1 confirms large fixed take-or-pay commitments, but the amounts are blank in this excerpt. It does not show any shortfall or that small upfront payments were the reason the company kept up.

reviews.rationale: Both labs held large raised cash balances, but the packet has no matched payment schedules for the second quarter of 2026. Nothing shows either lab could not pay obligations as they fell due, or that small signing payments were the only reason they kept up. The evidence does not settle the claim.

attribution.note: Zitron's own summary sentence. He draws on Ramp data but makes the conclusion himself.

semantics.note: Faithful. The non-tech qualifier and the no-clear-reversal clause are kept. Dropping 'catastrophic', an evaluative judgment, is appropriate.

contract.note: The plain reading (substantial spending is rare among non-tech firms, and nothing showed spending broadening at publication) is ordinary and fair. Excluding counts of paid adoption matches 'pay very much'.

evidence.note: Ramp, before the post: non-tech sectors closing the gap in paid adoption. That is an adoption count, not how much firms spend, so under the contract it does not contradict the claim.
Ramp's August update, published after the post: adoption still growing but more slowly, and per-employee spend by the top 1% fell. It gives no breakdown of spending by industry.

reviews.rationale: The packet has no industry-level breakdown of how much non-tech firms spend on AI in July 2026. The Ramp items show paid adoption widening outside tech, which the contract counts as insufficient, but not how many firms spend substantially. Neither condition is met.
